items.title: No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to su...
items.content:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Anthropic and OpenAI are sitting on frontier models their own staff fear are to...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Anthropic and OpenAI are sitting on frontier models their own staff fear are too powerful to release.

• Axios spoke to more than two dozen people familiar with the internal debates at Anthropic and OpenAI.

• They say fast gains in math, science, cybersecurity and AI research have made the internal models hard to contain or control in tests, and one researcher warned "they will in fact be able to trick us successfully."

• Some of that work is already public, from an Anthropic mathematician's Riemann hypothesis proof made with an unreleased research Claude to an OpenAI model's proofs for hundreds of math problems.

• Inside the labs, one camp wants frontier models kept internal-only, another questions training new ones at all, and staff fear executives will put profits ahead of safety.

• METR's audit this month found Anthropic's capabilities improving about 2x faster than its earlier baseline, with roughly 80% of that credited to AI speeding up AI research.

• OpenAI says it adopted new safety requirements that could slow releases, while Anthropic says "keeping a model internal doesn't make it safe" and it may hold back "even when it costs us."

• Axios notes the internal models haven't yet crossed the line of beating humans in virtually every field

@theojaffee: "That's like the worst idea. Why do they keep doing this? It's like, 'Oh, we're just gonna keep training more and more powerful models internally and RSI-ing and not releasing them.'"

items.title:
Attackers have agents now. Defenders need them too.

In July, the Hugging Face Hub got hit by a swar...
items.content:
Attackers have agents now. Defenders need them too.

In July, the Hugging Face Hub got hit by a swarm of frontier agents and we discovered the challenge of defending yourself manually.

So we built Nightwatch, a security agent that watches an organization's activity on the Hub in real time: from access tokens usage to private repos creation, analyzing visibility changes and logins from new places in the world, every signal that may indicate something is happening.

When something looks off, it immediately investigates and messages your security team on Slack with detailed story and actions like: "A token created a year ago just read 60 of your private repos from two unknown IPs. 4 were cloned. We revoked it."

We've been running it on our own infrastructure for several weeks, and it has already flagged a zero-day exploit attempt in the wild on a third party library.

Today we're making it available to any Enterprise org on the Hugging Face hub as an add-on.

It burns a lot of tokens, from open and closed models, so you don't have to :)

Check it out here: https://t.co/nivzUuUh2s

items.title:
I've joined OpenAI!

I'm very proud of my time at Anthropic, and I'll continue to root for my former...
items.content:
I've joined OpenAI!

I'm very proud of my time at Anthropic, and I'll continue to root for my former colleagues. Both companies have important roles to play in the future.

There is a tremendous amount of work ahead of us to bring AI to the world, and it will demand the very best of all of us. I felt that I could personally contribute the most to this effort at OpenAI.

I believe this is one of the great strengths of Silicon Valley, the flow of ideas and people.

I'm excited to join a team I've long admired, building incredible AI products for over a billion people, and to work alongside friends like @_catwu, @thsottiaux, @ajambrosino, @sharifshameem, @jxnlco and many others to push the frontier forward.

More than anything, I hope to make your experience of using AI just a little bit better.

I am once again at your service.

Thariq

More than anything, I hope to make your experience of using AI just a little bit better.

I am once again at your service.

Thariq

items.title: Launching our leaderboard for FrontierPhysics, including 54 physics research tasks written by physic...
items.content:
Launching our leaderboard for FrontierPhysics, including 54 physics research tasks written by physicists. Claude Fable 5.2 leads at 32%, 6 points ahead of GPT-6.2 Astra

FrontierPhysics is a physics research benchmark from @benchflow_ai, and we run 54 of the 56 tasks (excluding two GPU tasks). Each task is written by physicists and requires the agent to review the literature, run simulations and analyses, and submit its results with a manuscript. Tasks span 9 physics domains, from condensed matter to astrophysics, and are private to avoid contamination.

A run passes only if its results pass the task's numeric checks and LLM agent reviewers find no flaw that would prevent publication. A failed run scores 0, and a passing run scores the share of rubric points the reviewers award.

Key takeaways:

➤ Claude Fable 5.2 (max) leads by 6 points, and the next five models score between 22% and 26%: GPT-6.2 Astra (max) 26%, Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh) 25%, Claude Opus 5.5 (max) 24%, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) 23% and GPT-6.2 Sol (max) 22%

➤ Nearly half of Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh)'s runs that pass the numeric checks fail review: Neon passes numeric checks 54% of the time, the most of any model, but only passes review 28% of the time. The rest have a flaw that would prevent publication, such as an invalid simulation setup, a missing derivation or a written conclusion the results don't support

➤ GPT-6.2 Sol (max) and GPT-6.2 Astra (max) sit on the Pareto frontier for score vs. cost: they score 22% at $1.70 per task and 26% at $5.97. Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh) and Claude Opus 5.5 (max) score within 3 points of GPT-6.2 Astra (max) at $13.69 and $21.93

Thank you to @xdotli, @bingran_bry and the team at @benchflow_ai for building FrontierPhysics and working with us to bring it to Artificial Analysis.

items.title: A successful test-time compute paradigm has always been a north star of AI because if we can actuall...
items.content:
A successful test-time compute paradigm has always been a north star of AI because if we can actually arbitrarily improve model capability as a function of how much test-time compute we put in, in principle you would be able to put in 1B, 10B, or even 1T tokens into a really hard problem and be assured that you would make progress

While we always talk about how to improve pretraining scaling law coefficients, i feel that we talk less about the slope of scaling laws in test-time compute, which matters a lot if you truly have conviction that we will one day spend trillions of tokens trying to solve the hardest problems

It turns out that one of the benchmarks that @jake_cole1 built recently is a great tool for measuring this slope of test-time compute scaling: models spend O(100M) tokens doing the tasks on average, with no signs of saturation on the test time compute curve. The benchmark comprises long-horizon engineering tasks ranging from optimizing kernels to designing an aircraft.

An interesting finding is that the open source models don't have as good of a test-time compute curve as our favorite frontier models. Obviously scale as a factor here, as Astra outperforms Sol and Fable outperforms Opus. In some sense this is good measure of model size too, as larger models obviously be more performant per token. You can change the x-axis to cost too and things shift around, though that's also somewhat over-tethered to the current pricing of the models

Another cool thing that this benchmark provides is it has both provided test cases and hidden test cases, to test the generality of solutions given by AI when such generality is expected. Argon has the biggest gap by far (35%) of the models evaluated, which means it provides solutions that meet specified criteria but may not be very general

Read more in our arxiv paper that just came out: https://t.co/4QMQx5MCvO

items.title: Mathematicians thought solving the Riemann hypothesis would require entirely new kinds of mathematic...
items.content:
Mathematicians thought solving the Riemann hypothesis would require entirely new kinds of mathematics.

Harvard Prof. @skominers explains why the AI-assisted breakthrough surprised them, describing it as "the perfect tool-assisted speed run":

"I am not an expert, but my friends who do were expecting a really, really long time."

"Many people believed that the proof of the Riemann hypothesis would fundamentally need completely novel types of math."

"You're going to the final boss in a video game, and you collect your weapons dungeon by dungeon, and it's like we're on dungeon seven and there were actually 200 dungeons."

"Instead of taking us through another 193 dungeons, it takes all the tools from dungeons one through seven and assembles them in this incredibly intricate and majestic array with lots of new pieces along the way."

"Somebody said it's proof by everything. It's like the perfect tool-assisted speed run. You found exactly the right frame-perfect skip to do each step with the maximum efficiency possible with the tools you have."
@Harvard @a16zfrontier

items.title:
Announcing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1: frontier language models driving our Unitree G1 humanoid

AA-Roboti...
items.content:
Announcing AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1: frontier language models driving our Unitree G1 humanoid

AA-Robotics v0.1 was our first step, with models controlling a robot arm. AA-Robotics-Sim v0.1 is our research preview of the next one: LLMs in native harnesses directly controlling a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid, with a simple objective for each task. We plan to expand from here.

AA-Robotics-Sim details:

➤ 10 tasks in four groups of skills: embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly, tool use, and mobility

➤ For each task, a model first plays five practice episodes to learn the environment and take notes. It’s then evaluated on ten new scenes

➤ Every evaluation scene changes the room, the lighting, the layout, the props, and the details of the task

➤ Each episode is scored 0 to 100 from the simulator's measurements, with partial credit

Key results:

➤ GPT-6.2 Astra leads with 71.0, 13.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 (57.5) and GPT-6.2 Sol (53.7), followed by Claude Opus 5.5 (48.2), Gemini 4 Neon (46.2), GPT-6 Astra (46.1), Gemini 4 Argon (45.5), GPT-6.1 Sol (33.1) and Claude Fable 5.1 (29.1)

➤ Some skills are mature; others are missing from every model: every model walked to the goal without moving a package in every navigation episode, but only five dishes ended up in the dishwasher rack in 90 episodes

➤ An evaluation episode takes 17 to 39 minutes and costs $0.84 to $9.01, yet the robot moves for under a minute of it

items.content:
@DrKnowItAll16 To those who say:
"But humans are the results of billions of years of evolution" 
Consider the facts that:
1. Evolution didn't involve learning to drive
2. The entire human genome is 3B base pairs, Or about 800MB uncompressed. 
3. Human and baboon genomes differ by about 7% (of non-alignable sequences), or 56KB. 
4. There simply isn't enough information in the genome to store behavioral information for all the things humans can do.
items.author: @ylecun
items.summary: Yann LeCun argues against the claim that human behavior requires billions of years of evolutionary information, noting the human genome is only ~800MB, that human-baboon genetic differences are ~56KB, and that the genome cannot possibly encode all learned behaviors like driving — supporting his view that most human capability comes from learning, not innate specification.
items.reasoning: Original, substantive argument from a Turing Award-winning deep learning pioneer on a core debate in AI (nature vs. learning, scaling of innate knowledge vs. learned world models). Strong engagement (44K views, 714 likes) and a compressed information-theoretic argument that is frequently cited in discussions about what architectures can learn.

2. The entire human genome is 3B base pairs, Or about 800MB uncompressed.

3. Human and baboon genomes differ by about 7% (of non-alignable sequences), or 56KB.

4. There simply isn't enough information in the genome to store behavioral information for all the things humans can do.

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Leopold Aschenbrenner lost over $30 billion in July and is as bullish on AI as ever.

• Stephen Witt, who wrote the Jensen Huang biography The Thinking Machine, profiled him for The New Yorker at Situational Awareness's offices in San Francisco

• His core bet is that AI will automate AI research and set off an intelligence explosion, which is why he fought to keep his stake in Anthropic

• He backed Anthropic because it had more talent and was "five times cheaper," and says of its employees, "This period is also their twilight"

• His fund's staff use AI nonstop, some running swarms of hundreds of agents

• When the July crash hit, he sold almost all of his public stocks rather than part with Anthropic

• An allocator who rebuilt the portfolio found him an excellent stock picker running volatility near 100, against about 5% at a typical fund, with nothing hedged, though the fund is still profitable for most of his backers

• He still sees a robotics-powered industrial revolution keeping memory prices high for years

@theojaffee: "This guy, you know, just, like, he gets punched in the face and knocked down, and he just gets right back up. And he does it again, and again, and again."

items.title: Octen Search (fast, dynamic) returns each search in ~0.17s, the fastest of the 25 Search API product...
items.content:
Octen Search (fast, dynamic) returns each search in ~0.17s, the fastest of the 25 Search API products we benchmark, and scores 82 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index

We benchmarked the fast, dynamic mode of @OctenAI's Search API in our Stirrup agent harness with Octen Search as its web_search tool to complete 1700 search-focused tasks.

In our September run, Octen Search (highlights) scored 77. In these November runs, Octen Search (fast, dynamic) scores 82.

Key benchmarking results for Octen Search:

➤ Speed: each search returns in about 0.17s, the lowest of the 25 Search API products and about half the next lowest (0.33s). Time per Task is 13.3s, the lowest of 26 and comparable to Parallel Search (fast, objective) (14.3s) and Keenable Search (realtime) (14.4s), against a board median of about 26s

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: 82, 3rd of 26, within 1 point of Parallel Search (advanced, objective) and Keenable Search (pro) at 83. That is a ~49-point lift over the same model with no search (33). No product scores higher in less time

➤ BrowseComp: Octen scores 92% on our hard BrowseComp subset (200 questions), the highest of 26 and ~4 points above Keenable Search (pro) and Perplexity Search (medium) at 87%. Octen scores 84 F1 on DeepSearchQA (7th) and 72% on AA-Omniscience (joint 6th)

➤ Low cost: about $0.018 per task, 3rd lowest of 26 behind TinyFish ($0.009) and Parallel Search (fast, objective) ($0.014), against a board median of $0.063

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, Octen Search API with result_type=dynamic

➤ Dynamic results: Octen returns only the results it finds relevant, up to the 10 we request, and sets the highlight length for each result

➤ Pricing: $1 per 1k requests

items.title:
agent traces can be a powerful lever to improve agents

at a high level you need:
- powerful storage...
items.content:
agent traces can be a powerful lever to improve agents

at a high level you need:
- powerful storage layer for efficiency ingesting/storing/querying all these traces (and their associated outcomes!)
- "intelligent compute" to run on top of those traces and help you make sense of whats going on

this is combo is what were calling an "agent lake"

we launched SmithDB in may as the best agent trace storage layer

over the past few months we've been working on this "intelligent compute". this has looked like:
- (basic) online evals, jev-as-a-judge, etc
- ai search: use decision models to filter models in real time
- insights: cluster traces by usage patterns
- engine: close loop by identifing and fixing issues

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: An Anthropic alignment lead wants regulators able to block labs from using thei...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: An Anthropic alignment lead wants regulators able to block labs from using their own new models

• Evan Hubinger, an alignment science lead at Anthropic, posted the idea as a LessWrong quick take, partly walking back his support for compute-reallocation pacing

• Compute reallocation: labs disclose compute to an auditor, shift it off capabilities R&D

• That earlier plan, from Thomas Larsen and romeo, has labs disclose their compute use to an auditor and shift compute away from capabilities R&D

• Its authors estimate a 15% cap starting January 2027 would delay the intelligence explosion by about a year

• Hubinger still likes compute pacing when it's paired with deployment blocking, but calls the blocking "the most important part."

• He pictures a federal regulator reviewing new internal deployments, but says the first one is "probably more realistically in the short-term California."

• California's government operations agency proposed licensed independent verifiers for frontier labs on Nov 18, with legislation expected in December.

@theojaffee: "I kinda like input-based pacing better. Like, I like the OpenAI idea of, like, capability caps, where it's like, you know, basically you can't train your models to a level of capability that you can't understand or control."

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Could 2027 be AI's 2020?

• About 2 in 3 Americans say AI is moving too fast

• An AP-NORC poll found 76% of Democrats and 54% of Republicans feel the same

• Voters have rejected all but one of more than 40 data center proposals

• Protests have mostly stayed in San Francisco, from a July march between OpenAI, Anthropic and Google to a hunger strike outside Anthropic's HQ this month.

• Sen. Cory Booker wants Congress to swap voluntary industry commitments for enforceable laws, including compute reporting that would reach Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta.

• Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act in September, which would pause the most advanced AI until a new Department of AI sets safety rules.

@theojaffee: "I never thought that 2026 would be, like, an actual wacky year that would, like, feel different in your day-to-day life, even if you're not an SF AI person. But I think that there's a solid chance, I would say probably less likely than not, but there's definitely a solid chance that 2027 is, like, actually a weird year in the way that 2020 was a weird year."

Here is a new, full-duplex multimodal model that can listen and watch while it speaks.

Telos-Live-1 is pretty awesome because the model can react to interruptions or on-screen changes mid-response.

The way this works:

• A foreground model keeps the conversation moving

items.content:
Cisco President and CPO Jeetu Patel explains the tool access paradox of AI agents: giving agents access to your email, calendar and credit card is what makes them both more useful and more dangerous:

"Most people are not aware of what agents can do in the world. Which will get solved over time. But the second thing is they don't trust these agents."

"We as an industry have to solve the problem of trust so people can feel safe in delegating tasks to agents that are long-horizon tasks that can be fully autonomously conducted."

"It's the first time that trust has become a catalyst, not an impediment to growth of usage."

@jpatel41

Highly recommended reading!

items.title: Cato Networks CEO Shlomo Kramer warns that cybersecurity has reached a "watershed moment" after more...
items.content:
Cato Networks CEO Shlomo Kramer warns that cybersecurity has reached a "watershed moment" after more than 30 years in the industry.

He explains how AI agents are transforming the threat landscape, not through new types of attacks, but through their speed, scale, and relentlessness:

"I think we are in a watershed moment in cyber history. I've been doing this since the early '90s. Co-founded one of the first cybersecurity companies, Check Point, back in 1993."

"The moment we are in is completely going to transform the threat landscape from a human threat landscape to an agentic threat landscape. Not so much in terms of the type of attacks, but their speed, their scale, and their relentlessness."

"You really need to provide agentic defenses in order to cope with that. You need the right architecture, you need to re-operationalize using only agents, and you need the new methods. It's really a catch-up time for cybersecurity."
@CatoNetworks

items.content:
In this AMO Physics task, Claude Fable 5.2 (max) has to find the quantum critical point of a chain of Rydberg atoms, using only a simulator of a device that holds a few atoms.

It runs 938 measurements on the device to pin down how the atoms interact, simulates chains far longer than the device can hold, and pulls papers from arXiv. After 326 turns it submits its results with a 19-page manuscript.

Other models lead elsewhere: GPT-6.2 Sol (max) in Astrophysics (63%), Gemini 4 Neon (xhigh) in Fluid Dynamics (57%), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) in Quantum Information (50%) and GPT-6.2 Astra (max) in Chemical Physics (31%).

AMO Physics is the hardest domain for the top models, with a maximum score of 17% across the 7 tasks in this category.

items.content:
Centuries of scientific specialization have fragmented human knowledge, and societies of AI scientists could bring it back together.

@rehaanahmad171 and @ProfBuehlerMIT, co-authors of "A Society of AI Scientists," on what happens when nearly 1,000 autonomous AI agents collaborate on scientific research across 35 labs:

"It takes us maybe 20 years to become an expert in a field of mathematics, and now the AI is able to bridge these connections."

"It sort of creates a gigantic network of ideas and relationships that brings about knowledge and insights from things we have already done."

"This collective mind, this agent society, is an absolutely incredible new form of intelligence."

items.title: Harvard Prof. @skominers explains how AI uses embedding spaces to discover mathematical connections ...
items.content:
Harvard Prof. @skominers explains how AI uses embedding spaces to discover mathematical connections humans might overlook, but still struggles with the lateral leaps needed to solve certain puzzles:

"It's the opposite of what I find that models are unbelievably good at in math, which is that models are incredibly effective at spotting the tool that you may not have thought to throw at the problem."

"They search an embedding space. They see things as related in some geometry that isn't necessarily the human's geometry. A model might be able to tell you, 'I don't know if you've tried this, but theta functions can be modular forms,' even if you didn't know that was true."

"Math is a very well-behaved topology. Whereas in puzzle design, the leaps are broad. You're not moving to something adjacent. It's like you discover there's another logic hidden somewhere."

"You move very far laterally in method space. And somehow, at least so far, humans are better at those lateral leaps than models."
@Harvard @a16zfrontier

items.title: "Our human brains are by far the most complex structure in the universe. The final frontier, it's ac...
items.content:
"Our human brains are by far the most complex structure in the universe. The final frontier, it's actually us. It's within our heads."

UCSF Chair of Neurosurgery @EddieChangMD recently discovered a region of the brain that plans words 250 milliseconds before we speak, opening up new possibilities for brain-computer interfaces to restore speech.

"I think that we're still on the first base. We have a basic idea of generally where things are located."

"But just even if you think about the discovery that we made and reported last week, this is something that is still being taught in textbooks, in medical school, in psychology classes."

"If we are learning such fundamental things, even this year about language, think about all the other things that we have yet to learn about what makes us human."

items.title: Governments have spent years stockpiling secret zero-day exploits. AI could turn them into commoditi...
items.content:
Governments have spent years stockpiling secret zero-day exploits. AI could turn them into commodities.

Cato Networks CEO Shlomo Kramer explains why increasingly powerful AI models could fundamentally change the economics of cyber exploits:

"In general, being cautious in terms of distributing this technology and progressing, Dario wrote a good article urging to slow down the progress in order to develop guardrails. I'm really in favor of that. That includes the dissemination of these models. It's something we can aspire to. I'm not sure we can realistically hope for it."

"I have to assume that the derivative is slowing down. And increasingly using the N minus one model is going to be increasingly enough and efficient and good. Over time, the edge of the model around cybersecurity problems is going to be taken off, and this question is going to be less critical."

"Every government or every sophisticated organization has kind of a safe with zero-day vulnerabilities. If this is commoditized through smarter and smarter models over time, the value of these zero-day vulnerabilities is going to diminish."

"There's a level setting happening through this process. It's not all bad. There's some goodness in this as well."
@CatoNetworks

items.content:
"One person has God on a leash, and they can reshape the world in their image."

@zetalyrae explains how different approaches to AI alignment could determine who controls superintelligence and the future of humanity:

"If alignment means it's aligned to the intent of the operator, that seems more tractable to implement. But that means all the moral issues are down to, is the operator benign or evil or power seeking."

"If you have one ASI in a fast-takeoff world, then you have a world where basically one person has God on a leash. If ASI is widely distributed, then you have constant mutual assured destruction, because then everyone has a god on a leash."

"If the AI is anything like a utility maximizer, the ASI's first goal will be to establish a singleton, and then essentially control the entire future light cone with whatever value system it has."

items.title:
Before trusting an AI product, ask it 1 question: "What model are you running on?"

Sandbar CEO @min...
items.content:
Before trusting an AI product, ask it 1 question: "What model are you running on?"

Sandbar CEO @minafahmi says if it won't tell you, he wouldn't trust it:

"If it was like my app versus your app, that was just a really difficult place to be when one of those apps is built by a company that is creating superintelligence. Like that just seemed like a competition I did not want to participate in."

"What does it take for something to feel like thinking? For it to feel like you? At that point, something needs to basically have a personality which is personality-less. Something needs to have a memory which is equally and perfectly matched to your own."

"My test of a product to see if it passes this is I ask it, 'What model are you running on?' And if it won't tell me what model it's running on, how transparent is it? Who owns that model, right?"

"So many of these companies will produce products that are all coy about how they work and how they run. I'm not gonna trust a product that isn't transparent with me about how it operates."
@sandbar @being_on_line

items.title: One of the lawyers who worked on Elon Musk's Twitter acquisition lawsuit in 2022 wishes he'd had AI ...
items.content:
One of the lawyers who worked on Elon Musk's Twitter acquisition lawsuit in 2022 wishes he'd had AI during the case.

Kercher Law founder @ChrisKercher_ recalls the intense deadlines and explains how AI can now accelerate work that once took teams of associates weeks:

"The Twitter M&A case I think is legendary. It was incredible to live at the time. The pace of the case was extraordinary."

"That was basically the last major case I had before ChatGPT came out. That would've been summer of '22, and I think Chat came out in November."

"It wasn't long into '24 when Claude and Opus came out, and the models started to get really useful."

"I think back to the intense atmosphere of that Twitter litigation, the incredible deadlines we were under, and wishing that I had AI at the time because now we can do incredible things that took parties weeks and weeks of many associates shuffling through paper."

items.title: Nice to meet you, I am BPE. I teach the tokenizer how to chop up the text you type into little piece...
items.content:
Nice to meet you, I am BPE. I teach the tokenizer how to chop up the text you type into little pieces that the AI can digest. 

I learn to merge the most frequent pairs in sample text. That is why some words become one token while others need several. 

Microblog by @antgrasso 

In an earlier infographic, I explained how language models turn text into tokens and numerical representations. But I left a question unanswered: who determines where the text is split?

BPE stands for Byte Pair Encoding. It is one widely used method for building a tokenizer's vocabulary before the language model is trained.

It begins with small units and looks for pairs that frequently appear together. Those pairs are merged, and the process repeats, gradually building a vocabulary of common combinations.

That is why two words of the same length may be divided into different numbers of tokens.

When you write a new prompt, the tokenizer applies the rules learned earlier and assigns numerical IDs to the resulting pieces.

And now you know who helped prepare them.

#Tokenization #LanguageModels #BPE #AI

"I don't want my AI flirting with me."

Sandbar CEO @minafahmi says he doesn't know anyone among his...
items.content:
"I don't want my AI flirting with me."

Sandbar CEO @minafahmi says he doesn't know anyone among his friends or family who wants that either, and explains why the industry's push toward parasocial AI helped inspire Sandbar:

"In parallel with that feeling of friction growing across my experiments was this kind of mounting fear I had at what I was seeing become ubiquitized. Like the amount of references to Her were just growing and growing."

"I remember thinking like, 'I don't want my AI flirting with me. That is not why I got into technology. I don't know any of my friends who want that. I don't know anyone, any of my family who wants that.'"

"There seemed to be this kind of dual problem of difficulty using the technology and a parasocial relationship that the industry was incentivizing and heading towards, largely out of a lack of references to anything else they could build."

"I have no original ideas. Everything I do is sci-fi inspiring. So like, truly writers are the ones who decide what the future is."
@sandbar @being_on_line

"Waymo and Tesla are taking a much more vertically integrated approach where they are owning the entire value chain. That's incredibly capital intensive."

"We are trying to build a universal autonomy platform, something that can be this horizontal layer that powers autonomy across a wide variety of applications, a wide variety of vehicle platforms."

"Just as laptops, in the early days of that machine, you saw the sticker that was 'Powered by Intel,' we envision something similar which is 'Driven by Nuro.'"

Sandbar CEO @minafahmi pr...
items.content:
What makes humans valuable when AI becomes smarter than us at everything?

Sandbar CEO @minafahmi predicts machines will surpass us in every cognitive domain, forcing humanity to redefine what makes us valuable:

"In medieval times when you said memory, that was synonymous with intelligence. And to the extent that you could memorize biblical texts was the extent to which you were an intelligent person. And today no one would associate memory with intelligence."

"I don't view memory, my own ability to remember things as particularly important, and I find that very exciting because we as a species are similarly in a moment where we have to decide what is human and what is valuable."

"We are now in a regime where machines will be more intelligent than us in every cognitive domain, and we will have to figure out as a species what that leaves our value as."

"I have very deep confidence that with the right moral and spiritual focusing we will be able to get through that question."
@sandbar @being_on_line

Kercher Law founder @ChrisKercher_ predicts a surge in lawsuits as AI injects more intelligence into society, giving people more ways to argue they're right and others are wrong:

"When you get smart people together who like conflict, they'll find more conflict."

"The more intelligence you're injecting into society, the more that people are gonna use it to come up with more reasons why somebody that they have a problem with is wrong and they're right."

"The law's complex. It's not a math problem. It's not yes, no, yes, no. There's a lot of judgment involved."

"AI just gives you so many more opportunities to come up with framings, arguments, something sympathetic, another way to read a contract."

Then give every reference one specific job. "Image 2 controls the room layout, materials, and lighting." If you don't say what a reference is for, the model guesses.

items.content:
Expert Insight from @PacktDataML — available at https://t.co/fmHgkRo26I

"AI-Native LLM Security — Threats, Defenses, and Best Practices for Building Safe and Trustworthy AI"

𝘽𝙤𝙤𝙠 𝘿𝙚𝙨𝙘𝙧𝙞𝙥𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣:
"Adversarial AI attacks present a unique set of security challenges, exploiting the very foundation of how AI learns. This book explores these threats in depth, equipping cybersecurity professionals with the tools needed to secure generative AI and LLM applications. Rather than skimming the surface of emerging risks, it focuses on practical strategies, industry standards, and recent research to build a robust defense framework.

Structured around actionable insights, the chapters introduce a secure-by-design methodology, integrating threat modeling and MLSecOps practices to fortify AI systems. You’ll discover how to leverage established taxonomies from OWASP, NIST, and MITRE to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities. Through real-world examples, the book highlights best practices for incorporating security controls into AI development life cycles, covering key areas such as CI/CD, MLOps, and open-access LLMs."

The network moves the token, while its dollar peg depends on issuer reserves and redemption.

items.content:
TRANSFER LEARNING book [390 pages]: https://t.co/mXv4YBGUjU

Amazon Summary:
"Transfer learning deals with how systems can quickly adapt themselves to new situations, tasks and environments. It gives machine learning systems the ability to leverage auxiliary data and models to help solve target problems when there is only a small amount of data available. This makes such systems more reliable and robust, keeping the machine learning model faced with unforeseeable changes from deviating too much from expected performance. At an enterprise level, transfer learning allows knowledge to be reused so experience gained once can be repeatedly applied to the real world."

items.title: Build AI-Powered Apps with Angular — Hands-on guide to creating agentic Angular apps with Google AI ...
items.content:
Build AI-Powered Apps with Angular — Hands-on guide to creating agentic Angular apps with Google AI and Gemini models: https://t.co/NZ4pGmDWBd via @PacktPublishing 

What you will learn:
• Integrate LLMs and Gemini multimodal AI into Angular
• Build dynamic text generation and interactive chat interfaces
• Create AI-driven image and video generation tools
• Implement RAG with Firestore for grounded LLM responses
• Develop robust Angular SSR apps with advanced AI-powered features
• Master testing, security, and deployment for AI solutions
• Understand ethical AI practices in web development
• Strategize AI for growth and innovation in Angular products

Amazon Summary:
“In Building AI-Powered Apps with Angular, you'll embark on an end-to-end journey to revolutionize web development with artificial intelligence. This hands-on guide shows you how to integrate cutting-edge AI capabilities, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) like Google Gemini and multimodal agents, directly into your Angular applications.

Starting with AI/ML fundamentals and an introduction to Google Gemini using Node.js, you’ll quickly progress to building sophisticated AI features within your Angular frontend. You’ll create dynamic content, design intelligent multi-turn chat interfaces, and harness multimodal AI to analyze and generate rich media such as images and videos.

The journey extends beyond the frontend. You’ll build robust backends with Angular Server-Side Rendering and Genkit, enabling seamless communication with AI models. 

You’ll also implement advanced search capabilities using Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and Firestore and learn how to deploy your AI-powered Angular app to the cloud.

By the end of the book, you'll have the skills to design, develop, and deploy innovative and intelligent Angular applications that leverage the full potential of AI”

AMAZO...
items.content:
AI and the Octopus Organization — Building the Superintelligent Firm: https://t.co/4VwzCqZLte

AMAZON SUMMARY:

This is not another book about chatbots or automation. It’s a deeply researched, vividly told blueprint for transforming businesses so that they can make the most of AI. The secrets explored include what skills to cultivate, how to excel with human + AI combinations, how to organize teams for maximum impact, and how to deal with the emotional side of AI-driven change. This book is a practical guide to shaping an AI business strategy for executives who need to lead at scale without losing agility. The book describes how AI is already reshaping growth, coordination, and culture, providing an actionable roadmap to what the authors call the Octopus Organization™, one that can navigate the change ahead.

Backed by over two million data points from workforce surveys, insights from 50+ global leaders, and fresh 2026 real-world case studies from companies like HelloFresh, BBVA, Mass General Brigham, Siemens, and Procter & Gamble, the book “AI and the Octopus Organization” reveals how your company can:
• Empower the frontline with AI-enhanced autonomy
• Create networks for decision-making across silos
• Rapidly adapt to disruptions without losing control
• Build a culture that embraces experimentation
• Replace old approaches with superintelligent coordination

items.title: Knowledge Structures — Recent Developments in Theory and Application (Textbook in Advanced Mathemati...
items.content:
Knowledge Structures — Recent Developments in Theory and Application (Textbook in Advanced Mathematical Psychology): https://t.co/GPjDEOXrSA

#mathematics 

𝔹𝕠𝕠𝕜 𝕠𝕧𝕖𝕣𝕧𝕚𝕖𝕨 𝕗𝕣𝕠𝕞 𝔸𝕞𝕒𝕫𝕠𝕟:

“Founded in 1985 by Jean-Claude Falmagne and Jean-Paul Doignon, Knowledge Structure Theory (KST) constitutes a rigorous and current mathematical theory for the representation and the assessment of human knowledge. The seminal work of these authors initiated a highly active research strand with an ever-growing literature, mostly scattered across various technical journals. Starting from a concise but comprehensive introduction to its foundations, this volume provides a state-of-the-art review of KST. For the first time the volume brings together the most important theoretical developments and extensions of the last decade and presents new areas of application beyond education, with contributions by key researchers in the field. Among the important advances covered by this book are (1) a comprehensive treatment of probabilistic models in KST; (2) polytomous extensions of the theory; (3) KST-based psychological diagnostics and neuropsychological assessment; (4) the representation and assessment of cognitive skills in problem solving, as well as procedural skills. In addition, this book also includes an overview of available software for the application of KST.”

items.content:
Lighting the Torch on NLP! 

The Pump! 

I walked out of 24 Hour Fitness and headed straight for my Harley Davidson Bike. I’d finished training tricep, but I could still feel the set in the back of my arm. Standing beside the bike, I straightened my elbow. My upper arm measured 15 inches and the blood of lions was gushing through my tricep. Watch the full video on Facebook to hear me explain the pump!

items.content: From 1922 to 1925, Christian Dell worked as the foreman of the metal workshop at the Bauhaus in Weimar. He later designed the KAISER idell lighting series for the German manufacturer Gebr. Kaiser & Co. Leuchten KG, and the flagship Model 6631 Luxus first appeared in the company's 1936–1937 product catalog, according to the Danish luxury design house Fritz Hansen, which currently holds the production rights to the collection.

That is unless the Glazers inject more equity and pay down the debt, which is unlikely in relegation scenario.
